questions.question: In the early 2000s, Godrej Agrovet launched Godrej Aadhaar , a unique rural retail chain designed to move beyond simple product selling. Recognizing that rural consumers —primarily farmers—were often underserved and forced to travel long distances for quality goods, Godrej established "one-stop-shop" centers in large village clusters. Unlike traditional rural shops, Godrej Aadhaar provides a wide array of services: soil testing, crop advisory services, credit facilities through tie-ups with banks, and a retail floor selling everything from high -yield seeds and fertilizers to household a ppliances and FMCG products. By integrating knowledge with commerce, Godrej aimed to build a "circle of trust" with the rural farming community, positioning itself not just as a vendor, but as a partner in the farmer's economic growth. Questions: (a) Identify the primary segmentation bases used by Godrej Aadhaar. (b) Explain how targeting "progressive farmers" differs from mass marketing in rural areas. (c) Discuss the positioning strategy of Godrej Aadhaar as a "solution provider" versus a "product seller." (d) How does providing "intangible services" (like soil testing) support the rural marketing mix? . (CO4, An) (1x20=20) *******************

questions.question: A national bottled water brand launched a Cause-Related Marketing (CRM) campaign titled “Clean Water for Communities.” Under this initiative, the company pledged to donate ₹5 from every bottle sold to support safe drinking water projects in rural villages. The brand partnered with a reputed NGO to install water purification units and conduct hygiene awareness programs. The campaign was promoted through television advertisements, social media, and in-store displays highlighting how each purchase would help provide clean water. Customers responded positively, leading to increased sales and greater visibility for the cause. The NGO implemented the projects on the ground, monitored fund utilization, and shared impact reports with the company. However, some consumers questioned how much money actually reached the beneficiaries, while others felt such campaigns should be long-term initiatives rather than short promotional activities. You are required to: (a) Identify the social issue addressed in this case. (b) Explain how Cause-Related Marketing (CRM) is applied in this campaign. (c) Discuss the scope of CRM as reflected in this case (mention at least two areas). (d) Identify the type of Cause-Related Marketing used here and justify your answer. (e) State any two challenges of Cause-Related Marketing highlighted in this case.
questions.solution_html:
• (4 marks) each for each sub question.
  • (a) Social issue addressed
  • The social issue addressed in this case is lack of access to safe and clean drinking
  • water in rural communities, along with poor hygiene awareness.
  • (b) Application of Cause-Related Marketing (CRM)
  • Cause-Related Marketing is applied by linking product sales with a social cause. In this
  • case:
  • ➢ The company donates ₹5 for every bottle sold
  • ➢ Funds are used for rural water projects
  • ➢ Partnership with an NGO ensures implementation
  • ➢ Promotion highlights that each purchase contributes to the cause
  • o Thus, the campaign connects consumer buying behavior with social
  • impact.
  • (c) Scope of CRM (any two areas)
  • Social development:
  • Supports rural communities by providing clean drinking water and hygiene awareness.
  • Brand building and customer engagement:
  • Enhances brand image and attracts socially conscious consumers, leading to increased
  • sales.
  • (Other acceptable points: NGO collaboration, community welfare, corporate social
  • responsibility etc.)
  • (d) Type of CRM and justification
  • The type of CRM used is Transaction-based Cause-Related Marketing (or Purchase
  • triggered) Justification:
  • • Donation is directly linked to each product sale (₹5 per bottle)
  • • The contribution depends on consumer purchases
  • • Clear “buy-and-support” mechanism
  • (e) Two challenges of CRM highlighted in the case

questions.question: Purple Lilly Ltd. is a rural agricultural marketing company engaged in the cultivation and marketing of ornamental and commercial flowers in Munnar, Kerala, India. The company procures flowers from local cultivators and markets them across South India, particularly exporting fresh flowers to Tamil Nadu. In recent years, the company has observed the following developments: Rising demand for ornamental flowers in domestic and regional markets due to increased use in decoration, events, and religious purposes. Government initiatives promoting floriculture and supporting women’s rural entrepreneurship, leading to increased participation in flower cultivation. Growing adoption of greenhouse cultivation and modern farming techniques to improve flower quality and productivity. Expansion of online flower delivery platforms and increasing use of digital payment systems. Despite these opportunities, the company faces several challenges, including the short shelf life of flowers, seasonal fluctuations in demand, transportation delays, and lack of standardized grading and packaging practices. To enhance its market position, Purple Lilly Ltd. plans to establish cold storage facilities in different parts of Kerala and Tamil Nadu, improve packaging and preservation methods, develop strong branding strategies through celebrity endorsements, and create direct market linkages with buyers to reduce intermediaries.
